name: Incident resolved
description: The follow-up to an incident notice: it is fixed, this is what caused it, and this is what has changed so that it does not recur.

origin.note: Design: postmortem — a serif document between double rules, the timeline set in old-style figures, the cause named rather than described.

subject: Resolved: {{ impact_headline }}
preheader: The timeline, the cause named plainly, and what has changed so it does not recur.

eyebrow.description: Small label above the headline, classifying the document. This email is a record as much as a message, and the label is what makes it filable.

impact_headline.description: The same symptom named in the incident notice, so the two emails are obviously one thread. Do not soften it now that it is over.
impact_headline.example: Sending failed in the EU region

resolved_at.description: When impact actually ended for customers, not when the ticket was closed.

timezone.description: The timezone every time on this page is stated in, with its offset. The timeline is unreadable without it.

opening.description: What happened and who it hit, stated without euphemism. No 'some users may have experienced' — if sending failed for ninety minutes, write that sending failed for ninety minutes.
opening.example: For 90 minutes on 14 September, every message sent through our EU region failed. This was our fault, it was caused by a change we released, and no data was lost.

duration_value.description: How long customers were affected, set at display size because it is the number that will be quoted back to you. Leave empty if it cannot be stated honestly yet.

scope_value.description: The size of the blast radius as a figure — failed requests, affected accounts, delayed messages. Pair it with the duration so the impact is bounded in both directions.

timeline.description: The incident as `label` (the time) and `value` (what happened at it). Include the gap between the fault starting and you noticing it — leaving that row out is the tell that a postmortem is public relations.

example.value: A change to connection pooling was released to the EU region.

cause_text.description: The actual cause, in language a customer can follow. Name the mechanism rather than an abstraction: 'the pool was sized for one region and we ran two' beats 'an unexpected configuration issue'.
cause_text.example: A change to connection pooling assumed one database per region. The EU region runs two, so half of the pool pointed at a host that was not accepting writes.

cause_pending_text.description: Used when the cause is not established yet. Saying so plainly is more trustworthy than a guess that has to be corrected in a week, which is why this is a separate field rather than a hedge inside the one above.
cause_pending_text.default: We have not established the cause yet. We would rather tell you that than publish a guess and correct it next week.

remedies.description: The specific changes made, as `text` and optional `detail` saying whether each is already done or dated. 'We will improve our processes' is not one of these; a shipped guard rail with a date is.

example.text: Pool sizing is now derived from the region's host list

closing.description: The closing paragraph. An apology in your own words, and what a customer who lost something should do about it — a credit they must ask for is a credit you did not really offer.
closing.default: We are sorry. If this cost you a send you cannot repeat, reply to this email and we will credit the account without you having to make a case for it.

report_label.description: Label for the link to the full write-up.

report_url.description: The full public postmortem, for readers who want the engineering detail this email deliberately leaves out.
